blocks.text: Fine-tuning is not one single technique, it is a family of related approaches that differ in what data they use, what they optimize for, and how much of the model they actually change.

This topic maps out the main types you will encounter throughout the rest of this course, full fine-tuning, parameter efficient fine-tuning, instruction fine-tuning, alignment training, and a few related ideas, so later modules build on a clear shared vocabulary.
1. Not One Technique, A Family of Techniques

blocks.alt: Full fine-tuning branches into parameter efficient, instruction, and alignment fine-tuning

blocks.text: These types are not mutually exclusive stages you pick exactly one of, they answer different questions, how much of the model gets updated, what kind of data is used, and what behavior the training is trying to instill.
A real fine-tuning project often combines several of these ideas, for example using a parameter efficient method to run supervised fine-tuning on instruction style data.
2. Full Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Full fine-tuning updates every weight, which costs a lot of memory

blocks.text: Full fine-tuning updates every single weight in the model during training. It offers the most flexibility, since nothing is held fixed, but it requires storing gradients and optimizer state for the entire model, which becomes very expensive in memory as model size grows.
For very large models, full fine-tuning can require hardware far beyond what most individual teams have access to, which is the main reason parameter efficient methods became popular.
3. Parameter Efficient Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Frozen base weights combined with a small set of added parameters produce low memory cost

blocks.text: Parameter efficient fine-tuning, often shortened to PEFT, freezes most or all of the original model weights and instead trains a small number of newly added parameters, dramatically reducing the memory and compute needed to fine-tune.
LoRA is the most widely used method in this family, and gets an entire dedicated module later in this course given how central it has become to practical fine-tuning workflows.

blocks.text: 4. Instruction Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Raw instructions paired with expected responses build instruction-following ability

blocks.text: Instruction fine-tuning trains a model on pairs of instructions and correct responses, teaching it to follow a wide variety of directions given in natural language, rather than just continuing text in a plausible way.
This is the step that turns a raw pretrained model, which is only good at predicting the next token, into something that reliably behaves like a helpful assistant responding to a request.
5. Supervised Fine-Tuning on Task Specific Data

blocks.alt: Narrow task examples run through supervised fine-tuning to produce a task specific model

blocks.text: Supervised fine-tuning, often shortened to SFT, is the general term for training on a labeled dataset of input, output pairs for a specific task, whether that task is classification, summarization, or a custom company workflow.

Most of what earlier topics in this module discussed, teaching a model your support tone or your document format, is a form of supervised fine-tuning, and this course dedicates an entire module to it directly after the dataset preparation modules.
6. Alignment Fine-Tuning, RLHF and DPO

blocks.alt: Human preferences drive alignment training toward a safer, more helpful model

blocks.text: Alignment training is a distinct category focused less on task accuracy and more on shaping the model overall behavior toward being helpful, honest, and safe, typically using human preference data rather than simple correct or incorrect labels.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback, RLHF, and direct preference optimization, DPO, are the two most common approaches here, both covered in depth in this course dedicated Alignment Training module.

blocks.title: Alignment answers a different question
blocks.content: Where supervised fine-tuning asks what is the correct output, alignment training asks which of several plausible outputs a human would actually prefer, a subtly different and important distinction.

blocks.text: 7. Continued Pretraining, A Related but Different Idea

blocks.alt: Continued pretraining on broad domain data is compared against fine-tuning on narrow labeled data

blocks.text: Continued pretraining takes a pretrained model and keeps training it, using the same broad, unlabeled style of data as original pretraining, but focused on a specific domain, for example a large collection of legal documents, without task specific labels.

This differs from fine-tuning in an important way, continued pretraining still uses the broad next token prediction objective, it simply narrows the domain of the data, while fine-tuning typically uses labeled, task shaped examples to steer specific behavior.
8. Multi-Task Fine-Tuning

Multi-task fine-tuning trains a single model on a mixture of several different tasks at once, rather than specializing narrowly on just one, aiming for a model that handles a family of related jobs well without needing a separate fine-tuned copy for each.
This tradeoff, breadth across several tasks versus depth on exactly one, comes up repeatedly in later modules when deciding how narrow or broad a fine-tuning dataset should be.
9. Choosing Among These Types

In practice, most fine-tuning projects blend more than one of these ideas, for instance running supervised fine-tuning using a parameter efficient method like LoRA, on a dataset built in the instruction style, sometimes followed by an alignment pass afterward.

items: Limited hardware available, lean toward parameter efficient methods rather than full fine-tuning
Task is a specific input to output mapping, supervised fine-tuning is the natural fit
Goal is broad helpfulness and safety, not just one task, alignment training becomes relevant
Need the model to absorb a large body of domain text before task training, consider continued pretraining first

blocks.text: Worked Example

A team building a legal assistant first runs continued pretraining on a large collection of unlabeled legal documents, so the model absorbs legal vocabulary and phrasing broadly, without any specific task defined yet.

They then run supervised fine-tuning using a parameter efficient method on three thousand labeled document summarization examples, teaching the model the specific summarization task on limited hardware.

Finally, they run a short alignment pass using human preference comparisons, so the model reliably prefers cautious, well hedged legal language over confident but potentially incorrect statements. Each stage used a different type of fine-tuning for a different purpose.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating full fine-tuning as the default without checking whether a parameter efficient method would work just as well for less cost
Confusing continued pretraining, which uses broad unlabeled data, with supervised fine-tuning, which uses labeled task data
Skipping instruction fine-tuning and expecting a raw pretrained model to follow directions reliably
Assuming alignment training and supervised fine-tuning solve the same problem, when they optimize for different things

blocks.text: Practice

For a fine-tuning project you might realistically attempt, decide which of these types actually applies, full or parameter efficient, instruction style or narrow task style, and whether an alignment pass would matter for your use case.
Key Takeaway

Fine-tuning is a family of techniques, not a single method, and full versus parameter efficient describes how much of the model changes, while instruction, supervised, and alignment fine-tuning describe what kind of behavior the training is actually shaping.
